Classical attributive 〜ki (〜き) is the literary equivalent of modern 〜i (〜い) in i-adjective attributive position. Modifies a following noun: utsukushiki hito (<ruby>美<rt>うつく</rt></ruby>しき<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>) 'a beautiful person' (modern: utsukushii hito). Survives in poetry, song lyrics, formal / archaic prose, and idiomatic / classical compounds: kanashiki sadame (<ruby>悲<rt>かな</rt></ruby>しき<ruby>定<rt>さだ</rt></ruby>め) 'a sad fate'.

The classical paradigm split adjective forms into predicative (sentence-final, 〜shi) and attributive (modifying a noun, 〜ki). Modern Japanese collapses both into 〜i. The classical 〜ki is purely a register marker now — using it signals literary / archaic / song-like style.

Compare with classical 〜nu (negative predicative, batch3b), 〜zu (negative continuative, batch4a), 〜naki (negative attributive, batch4a). All are part of the surviving classical paradigm. 〜ki is one of the most commonly encountered in song titles and lyrics: utsukushiki hibi (beautiful days), kanashiki yoru (sad night). Recognising it as 'just literary 〜i' unlocks much of song-lyric reading.

name: Emphatic ha (は) in negative (〜ku wa nai) — softened 'not even'

explanation.en:
Emphatic 〜は (〜は) inserted into a negative construction softens or focuses the negation. Most commonly seen as 〜ku wa nai (〜くはない) or 〜taku wa nai (〜たくはない), where 〜は precedes the nai. takunai (don't want to) → tabe-taku wa nai (<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べたくはない) 'I don't necessarily want to eat (it)'. The 〜は makes the negation contrastive — implying 'not X, but something else / not exactly X'.

The structure introduces nuance: with 〜は, the negation becomes scoped, qualified, or contrastive. Compare bare 〜nai (flat denial) with 〜wa nai (focused denial): kanashii — 'sad'; kanashi-ku-wa-nai — 'not sad (per se / not in the way you might think)'. Often paired with 〜ga (but) for explicit contrast: takunai ga, tabenakute mo ii (don't necessarily want to eat, but it's fine not to).

Compare with 〜ja nai (negative copula), 〜nai de (without doing), and the simple 〜nai. Emphatic は is a subtle but characteristic Japanese grammatical move — the kind of nuance that distinguishes intermediate from beginner-level Japanese. Used heavily in lyrics, novels, and any context wanting hedged or scoped denial.

• tabe-taku wa nai (<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べたくはない) — "don't necessarily want to eat"
• ikitaku wa nai (<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きたくはない) — "don't really want to go"
• shiritakunai wa nai (<ruby>知<rt>し</rt></ruby>りたくはない) — "don't really want to know"
• ureshikunai wa nai (<ruby>嬉<rt>うれ</rt></ruby>しくはない) — "not exactly happy"

name: Emphatic prefix ma〜 (真っ〜) — intensified adjective

explanation.en:
Emphatic prefix 〜ma (真っ〜 / まっ〜) attaches to color and intensity adjectives or nouns to mean 'pure / completely / absolutely X'. Most common with colors: makka (<ruby>真<rt>まっ</rt></ruby><ruby>赤<rt>か</rt></ruby>) 'bright red / crimson'. masshiro (<ruby>真<rt>まっ</rt></ruby><ruby>白<rt>しろ</rt></ruby>) 'pure white'. Also with darkness, brightness, and other absolutes: makura (<ruby>真<rt>まっ</rt></ruby><ruby>暗<rt>くら</rt></ruby>) 'pitch dark', massaki (<ruby>真<rt>まっ</rt></ruby><ruby>先<rt>さき</rt></ruby>) 'foremost'.

The 真 (ma, 'true / pure') prefix intensifies — the modified property is at its absolute maximum. Often attaches with the small っ (sokuon) for euphonic emphasis: ma+ + akai → makka. Treats the whole compound as a na-adjective: makka na sora (<ruby>真<rt>まっ</rt></ruby><ruby>赤<rt>か</rt></ruby>な<ruby>空<rt>そら</rt></ruby>) 'a crimson sky'.

Common compounds (mostly fixed): makka, masshiro, makkuro (<ruby>真<rt>まっ</rt></ruby><ruby>黒<rt>くろ</rt></ruby> 'jet black'), maaomi or massao (<ruby>真<rt>まっ</rt></ruby><ruby>青<rt>さお</rt></ruby> 'deep blue / pale'), masuguru (<ruby>真<rt>まっ</rt></ruby><ruby>直<rt>す</rt></ruby>ぐ 'straight'), maatarashii (<ruby>真<rt>ま</rt></ruby><ruby>新<rt>あたら</rt></ruby>しい 'brand new'). Beloved in lyrics for vivid imagery: makka na sora at sunset, masshiro na yuki (pure white snow). Compare with prefix 〜chou (<ruby>超<rt>ちょう</rt></ruby>, 'super', casual) and 〜oo (<ruby>大<rt>おお</rt></ruby>, 'great').

name: Negative imperative 〜nai de (〜ないで) — please don't

explanation.en:
Negative imperative 〜nai de (〜ないで) attaches to a verb's nai-stem to express a soft prohibition or polite negative request — 'please don't X'. Distinct from the rough 〜na imperative (batch4a, 'don't!'), 〜nai de carries gentleness and request flavour. naka-nai de (<ruby>泣<rt>な</rt></ruby>かないで) "please don't cry". Polite extension: 〜nai de kudasai (please don't, formally).

Two readings: (a) Soft prohibition / request — most common, used in songs, gentle commands, intimate speech. (b) Manner / accompaniment — 'without doing X' — kakanai de henji shita (<ruby>書<rt>か</rt></ruby>かないで<ruby>返事<rt>へんじ</rt></ruby>した) 'replied without writing'. Context disambiguates; the soft-imperative reading often ends a sentence, the 'without' reading connects clauses.

Compare with 〜zu ni (literary 'without doing', batch1), 〜na (rough imperative, batch4a), 〜nakute (negative te-form connector), and 〜nai de kudasai (polite formal request). 〜nai de is the everyday gentle prohibition — a J-pop staple for vulnerable pleas: ika nai de (don't go), wasure nai de (don't forget).

How it works: English past tense narrates events that already happened. Regular verbs add -ed; irregular verbs have unique forms. In Japanese, the た-form (ta-form) serves the same purpose.

Example from this song: 'lost', 'gave', 'changed' — English past tenses telling a story of loss and transformation.

Japanese equivalents:
• 'lost' → 失った (ushinatta, from 失う/ushinau, 'to lose')
• 'gave' → 与えた (ataeta, from 与える/ataeru, 'to give')
• 'changed' → 変わった (kawatta, from 変わる/kawaru, 'to change')

Note: Japanese past tense (た-form) follows consistent rules once you know the verb group. Godan verbs have sound changes (く→いた, ぐ→いだ, etc.), while ichidan verbs simply replace る with た.

How it works: English present continuous ('am + verb-ing') expresses actions happening right now. Japanese uses 〜ている (te-iru) for the same purpose — て-form + いる.

Example from this song: 'I'm crying', 'I'm standing' — expressing immediate, ongoing emotional states.

Japanese equivalents:
• 'I'm crying' → 泣いている (naiteiru, from 泣く/naku, 'to cry')
• 'I'm standing' → 立っている (tatteiru, from 立つ/tatsu, 'to stand')
• 'I'm fighting' → 戦っている (tatakatteiru, from 戦う/tatakau, 'to fight')

Note: In casual speech, ている → てる: 泣いてる (naiteru). In more casual speech, even てる can contract: 何してんの？ (nani shiten no?, 'what are you doing?').

name: Question word + mo + negative — universal negation

explanation.en:
Question word + も + negative is a paired construction expressing universal negation — 'no(thing) / no one / never / nowhere'. The question word marks the universal scope; mo (も, 'also / even') extends it to all instances; the negative predicate denies them all. dare mo inai (<ruby>誰<rt>だれ</rt></ruby>もいない) 'no one is here'. nani mo nai (<ruby>何<rt>なに</rt></ruby>もない) 'there's nothing'.

Question words and their universal-negation expansions: dare mo (no one), nani mo (nothing), doko mo (nowhere), itsu mo (used in negative for 'never'... actually itsu mo means 'always'; for 'never' use itsu mo 〜nai or kesshite 〜nai), donna 〜mo (no kind of), dochira mo (neither). The negation MUST be at the end — without it, the same surface forms mean 'everyone / everything / everywhere'.

Compare with bare 〜nai, kesshite (batch4b — 'never' adverb), zenzen 〜nai (not at all). The question-word + も + negative pattern is the most productive way to express universal absence in Japanese. Mastery is essential — many beginner errors come from forgetting that mo + negative means 'NONE' rather than 'all'.

• nani mo nai (<ruby>何<rt>なに</rt></ruby>もない) — "there's nothing"

Sentence-final 〜sa (〜さ) is a masculine assertive softener / reflective marker. Attaches to plain-form sentences. Means 'X, you know / X, that's the thing'. Less aggressive than 〜zo / 〜ze; more reflective and conversational. wakaru sa (<ruby>分<rt>わ</rt></ruby>かるさ) "I get it (don't worry)". Often used to console or to assert with quiet confidence.

Stereotypically male in modern Japanese, though some women use it in casual / friendly speech. The 〜sa softens an assertion that would otherwise be flat or harsh. Often paired with self-pep-talk verbs: daijoubu sa (<ruby>大丈夫<rt>だいじょうぶ</rt></ruby>さ) "it's fine, you know". Sometimes attaches to nouns / na-adjectives: yume sa (<ruby>夢<rt>ゆめ</rt></ruby>さ) "it's a dream, see".

Compare with 〜zo (self-pep), 〜ze (outward rallying), 〜yo (neutral assertion), 〜no sa (explanatory + sa, batch4a). Sentence-final 〜sa sits in the gentle-masculine reflective zone. In ballads and slow songs, it adds quiet self-knowledge. In dialogue, it tells the listener 'this is how it is, don't worry / I'm sure'.

name: Verb-stem + ni + iku / kuru (〜に行く / 〜に来る) — go / come to do X

explanation.en:
Verb-stem + ni + iku / kuru (〜に<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>く / 〜に<ruby>来<rt>く</rt></ruby>る) attaches the masu-stem of a verb + に + a motion verb (行く 'go' or 来る 'come') to express purpose of motion — 'go / come (in order) to do X'. tabe ni iku (<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べに<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>く) 'go to eat'. au ni kuru (<ruby>会<rt>あ</rt></ruby>いに<ruby>来<rt>く</rt></ruby>る) 'come to meet'.

Distinct from 〜tame ni (in order to, batch2 — abstract purpose) and 〜you to suru (try to, batch4a — effortful intent). 〜ni iku / 〜ni kuru is specifically about MOVEMENT plus purpose. The motion verb specifies direction (away from / toward speaker).

Also accepts noun + ni + iku for shopping / events: kaimono ni iku (<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>い<ruby>物<rt>もの</rt></ruby>に<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>く) 'go shopping', tabe ni iku (go to eat), see ni iku (go to look). Verbs of leisure / errand / meeting are most common. Past forms 〜ni itta / 〜ni kita carry the same purpose meaning. Compare with 〜te kuru ('come having done X' — done elsewhere then return).

name: 〜ga mama ni (〜がままに) — as one pleases / freely

explanation.en:
〜ga mama ni (〜がままに) attaches to a plain-form verb (often non-volitional or passive). Means 'as one pleases / freely / left to itself'. omou ga mama ni (<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>うがままに) 'as one wishes / as the heart pleases'. The 〜ga marks the subject of the action; mama (まま, 'state / as is', batch2) is preserved as a noun-like marker; ni (に) makes it adverbial.

Highly literary / formal — common in songs, prose, and elevated speech. Carries connotations of unrestrained naturalness or destiny: kaze no fuku ga mama ni (<ruby>風<rt>かぜ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>吹<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>くがままに) 'as the wind blows / wherever the wind takes us'. Often used to express surrender to natural forces or one's own desires.

Compare with batch2's 〜mama (state-preserving 'as is'), 〜jiyuu ni (freely — neutral adverb), and 〜you ni (manner / purpose, batch3a / batch2). 〜ga mama ni is the elevated 'as it wills' marker — in lyrics, evokes flow, destiny, or the surrender of agency. Pairs well with verbs of natural motion (kaze ga fuku, mizu ga nagareru).

name: 〜janai ka (〜じゃないか) — isn't it? / how about

explanation.en:
〜janai ka (〜じゃないか) attaches to plain-form sentences. Combines the negative copula 〜janai with the question particle 〜ka. Means "isn't it? / X, right? / how about X?". Used both for confirmation-seeking ('X, right?') and for offering / suggesting ('how about X?'). ii janai ka (いいじゃないか) "isn't it fine?".

Two main flavours: (a) Confirmation — softer 'isn't it?' than direct asking, often inviting agreement. wakatta janai ka (<ruby>分<rt>わ</rt></ruby>かったじゃないか) "you understood, right?". (b) Suggestion / invitation — 'why not X / how about X' — yatte miyou janai ka (やってみようじゃないか) "let's try, why not". Stereotypically male in modern speech but used by all genders in casual contexts.

Polite form: 〜janai desu ka (〜じゃないですか). Casual contractions: 〜jan (〜じゃん, very casual), 〜janee ka (〜じゃねえか, rough male). Compare with 〜darou (probably / right?, batch3a), 〜yo ne (gentle agreement-seeking), 〜deshou (polite seeking confirmation). 〜janai ka is the warm 'isn't it?' — slightly softer than direct interrogation, often friendly.

〜kashira (〜かしら) is the feminine equivalent of 〜kana (batch3b, 'I wonder'). Attaches to plain-form sentences. Self-directed pondering with feminine softness. ame ga furu kashira (<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>るかしら) "I wonder if it'll rain". Stereotypically female; men using it sound playful / archaic / character-affected.

Same functional range as 〜kana: self-wonder, soft request, soft suggestion. Combined with 〜nai for wishful tone: konai kashira (<ruby>来<rt>こ</rt></ruby>ないかしら) 'I wonder if (X won't come) / I hope (X comes)'. Slightly more reserved / elegant register than 〜kana — appears in older female speech, romantic / nostalgic songs, and feminine literary voice.

Compare with 〜kana (neutral / male / female), 〜n darou (more direct conjecture, batch3b), 〜darou ka (formal 'I wonder'). 〜kashira is the feminine wonder marker — using it characterises the speaker as female (especially older or refined). In modern young female speech, 〜kana has largely replaced it.

name: 〜koto ga dekiru (〜ことができる) — be able to do (analytic potential)

explanation.en:
〜koto ga dekiru (〜ことができる) is the analytic potential — alternative to the morphological potential form (kanoukei, batch4a). Attach to V-dictionary form + koto + ga dekiru. taberu koto ga dekiru (<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べることができる) 'be able to eat'. The structure literally reads 'the act of eating is possible'.

More formal and analytical than the synthetic potential form (taberareru). Often preferred in writing, polite speech, and contexts where the action is a discrete capability rather than a concrete instance: nihongo wo hanasu koto ga dekiru ('be able to speak Japanese') vs. nihongo ga hanaseru (same meaning, more conversational).

Conjugates as a regular ichidan-like verb: 〜koto ga dekita (was able), 〜koto ga deki nai (cannot), 〜koto ga dekire ba (if able). The negative form is widely used in lyrics for impossibility expressions: tsutaeru koto ga deki nai (<ruby>伝<rt>つた</rt></ruby>えることができない) "cannot convey". Compare with synthetic potential (batch4a — concise, conversational), 〜eru / 〜rareru (same).

〜sura (〜すら) attaches to nouns to mean 'even (X) / not even X'. Formal / written / emphatic 'even', stronger than 〜mo (も) and 〜sae (さえ, batch2). The implication is 'X is unexpected at this level / X is the most extreme case'. kodomo sura wakaru (<ruby>子供<rt>こども</rt></ruby>すら<ruby>分<rt>わ</rt></ruby>かる) 'even a child gets it'.

Distinct from 〜sae (batch2) by register: 〜sura is more literary / formal / dramatic; 〜sae is everyday / colloquial. Both express 'even', but 〜sura is reserved for stronger emphasis or written contexts. Often paired with negation for 'not even': namida sura denai (<ruby>涙<rt>なみだ</rt></ruby>すら<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>ない) 'not even tears come'.

Compare with 〜sae (everyday 'even'), 〜made (even / going so far as, batch3a), 〜datte (casual 'even', batch2). 〜sura is the high-register 'even' marker — perfect for elevated lyrics, formal claims, and any context wanting weighty emphasis. In song lyrics it's used for dramatic emphasis: kotoba sura mou ie nai (<ruby>言葉<rt>ことば</rt></ruby>すらもう<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>えない) 'I can't even speak words anymore'.

• namida sura denai (<ruby>涙<rt>なみだ</rt></ruby>すら<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>ない) — "not even tears come"
• kao sura mire-nai (<ruby>顔<rt>かお</rt></ruby>すら<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>れない) — "can't even see (their) face"
• namae sura wasureta (<ruby>名前<rt>なまえ</rt></ruby>すら<ruby>忘<rt>わす</rt></ruby>れた) — "I've forgotten even (their) name"
• yume sura mire-nai (<ruby>夢<rt>ゆめ</rt></ruby>すら<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>れない) — "can't even dream"
• ichi-byou sura mu-da ni shi-nai (<ruby>一秒<rt>いちびょう</rt></ruby>すら<ruby>無<rt>む</rt></ruby><ruby>駄<rt>だ</rt></ruby>にしない) — "won't waste even a second"
• kanaru sura yurusare-nai (<ruby>叶<rt>かな</rt></ruby>うすら<ruby>許<rt>ゆる</rt></ruby>されない) — "not even allowed to come true"
• ai sura wakaranai (<ruby>愛<rt>あい</rt></ruby>すら<ruby>分<rt>わ</rt></ruby>からない) — "I don't even understand love"
• ima sura tooku ni kanjiru (<ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby>すら<ruby>遠<rt>とお</rt></ruby>くに<ruby>感<rt>かん</rt></ruby>じる) — "even now feels far away"
• kotoba sura mou ie nai (<ruby>言葉<rt>ことば</rt></ruby>すらもう<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>えない) — "I can't even speak words anymore"
• boku no namae sura kikoenai (<ruby>僕<rt>ぼく</rt></ruby>の<ruby>名前<rt>なまえ</rt></ruby>すら<ruby>聞<rt>き</rt></ruby>こえない) — "can't even hear my name"
• te wo nigiru koto sura yurusarenai (<ruby>手<rt>て</rt></ruby>を<ruby>握<rt>にぎ</rt></ruby>ることすら<ruby>許<rt>ゆる</rt></ruby>されない) — "not even allowed to hold (your) hand"
• kanji sura kakenai (<ruby>漢字<rt>かんじ</rt></ruby>すら<ruby>書<rt>か</rt></ruby>けない) — "can't even write kanji"

<!-- v2-romaji-primary -->

How it works: ことさえも (koto sae mo) combines the nominalizer こと (koto) with the emphatic particle さえも (sae mo, 'even'). It means 'even the act of doing X.'

Example from this song: The song uses ことさえも to emphasize that even the action itself is noteworthy or surprising.

More examples:
• 歩くことさえも辛い (aruku koto sae mo tsurai, 'even just walking is painful')
• 笑うことさえも忘れた (warau koto sae mo wasureta, 'even forgot how to laugh')
• 生きることさえも怖い (ikiru koto sae mo kowai, 'even living itself is scary')

Note: こと turns the verb into a noun ('the act of doing'). さえも adds 'even.' Together: 'even the very act of X.' This creates strong dramatic emphasis — if even this fundamental action is affected, the situation is extreme.

How it works: ことで (koto de) means 'by doing ~' — it indicates the means or method by which something is achieved. こと (koto) nominalizes the verb, and で (de) marks the means.

Example from this song: The song uses ことで to express how something is achieved — 'by (doing this action), (this result happens).'

More examples:
• 練習することで上手になる (renshuu suru koto de jouzu ni naru, 'by practicing, you get better')
• 話すことで気持ちが楽になる (hanasu koto de kimochi ga raku ni naru, 'by talking, you feel better')
• 読むことで世界が広がる (yomu koto de sekai ga hirogaru, 'by reading, your world expands')

Note: こと turns a verb into a noun (nominalizer). Adding で means 'by means of that action.' This is useful for explaining cause-and-effect or methods.

Formal/literary alternative to 〜ないで or 〜ずに ('without V-ing'). Verb-dictionary form + ことなく. Common in formal writing, lyrics, and speeches. Zetsu Zetsu's 絶やすことなく ('without letting it die out') describes a sustained action characterized by a lack: 'connect the threads forever, without ever letting them die.' The construction is more deliberate-sounding than the everyday 〜ないで.
explanation.es: Alternativa formal/literaria a 〜ないで o 〜ずに ('sin V'). Forma de diccionario del verbo + ことなく. Común en escritura formal, letras y discursos. El 絶やすことなく ('sin dejar que se extinga') de Zetsu Zetsu describe una acción sostenida caracterizada por una falta: 'conectar los hilos para siempre, sin dejar nunca que mueran'. La construcción suena más deliberada que el cotidiano 〜ないで.
explanation.pt-BR: Alternativa formal/literária a 〜ないで ou 〜ずに ('sem V'). Forma de dicionário do verbo + ことなく. Comum em escrita formal, letras e discursos. O 絶やすことなく ('sem deixar morrer') de Zetsu Zetsu descreve ação sustentada caracterizada por uma falta: 'conectar os fios pra sempre, sem nunca deixar morrer'. Construção soa mais deliberada que o cotidiano 〜ないで.

explanation.en:
How it works: Place ことは (koto wa) after a verb's dictionary form and follow with ない (nai). This creates a firm statement: 'I will never do X' or 'there is no doing X'.

Example from this song: The lyrics use this pattern to express a firm resolve — there's something the speaker absolutely won't do.

More examples:
• 諦める (akirameru, 'to give up') → 諦めることはない (akirameru koto wa nai, 'there's no giving up / I won't give up')
• 後悔する (koukai suru, 'to regret') → 後悔することはない (koukai suru koto wa nai, 'there's nothing to regret')
• 忘れる (wasureru, 'to forget') → 忘れることはない (wasureru koto wa nai, 'I'll never forget')

Note: This sounds more reflective and decisive than simply using ない. It turns the action into an abstract concept (こと = 'the act of') and negates it entirely.

name: 〜ことも＋なく (koto mo naku - without even)

explanation.en:
Expresses that something does not happen, with emphasis on "not even." It combines こと (koto, "the act of") + も (mo, "even") + なく (naku, "without").

How it works:
Verb dictionary form + ことも + なく. It means "without even [doing X]."

Example from this song:
時が止まることもなく (toki ga tomaru koto mo naku, "Without time ever stopping")

More examples:
- 振り返ることもなく去った (furikaeru koto mo naku satta, "Left without even looking back")
- 休むこともなく働いた (yasumu koto mo naku hataraita, "Worked without even resting")
- 迷うこともなく答えた (mayou koto mo naku kotaeta, "Answered without even hesitating")

How it works: Use the causative te-form させて (sasete) to request permission to do something — 'let me do X' or 'allow me to do X'.

Example from this song: いさせて (isasete) = 'let me be here / let me stay' — from いる (iru, 'to be/exist') → いさせる (isaseru, causative) → いさせて (isasete, 'let me be')

More examples:
• 行く (iku, 'to go') → 行かせて (ikasete, 'let me go')
• やる (yaru, 'to do') → やらせて (yarasete, 'let me do it')
• 言う (iu, 'to say') → 言わせて (iwasete, 'let me say')

Note: させて is the causative form used as a request. For -ru verbs: る→させて. For -u verbs: change to あ-row + せて. する→させて, 来る→来させて (kosasete). Adding ください makes it polite: 行かせてください.

How it works: Take the verb masu-stem and add そう (sou, 'looks like') + で (de, connecting) + the potential negative. This expresses frustrated expectation — 'it seems like it would X, but it won't/can't'.

Example from this song: 壊れそうで壊せない (kowaresou de kowasenai) = 'seems like it would break but I can't break it' — from 壊れる (kowareru, 'to break') → 壊れそう (kowaresou, 'looks like it'll break') + で + 壊せない (kowasenai, 'can't break')

More examples:
• 届く (todoku, 'to reach') → 届きそうで届かない (todokisou de todokanai, 'seems within reach but can't reach')
• できる (dekiru, 'can do') → できそうでできない (dekisou de dekinai, 'seems doable but can't do it')

Note: This pattern captures a relatable frustration — something that appears possible but isn't. It's a powerful emotional expression in song lyrics.

い-adjective stem (or な-adjective + そう) + そうに describes appearing or seeming a certain way: 残念そうに 'with a regretful look', 嬉しそうに 'looking happy'. Always describes externally observable expression, never the speaker's own feeling.
explanation.es: Raíz del adjetivo い (o な-adjetivo + そう) + そうに describe apariencia: 残念そうに 'con cara de pena', 嬉しそうに 'pareciendo feliz'. Siempre describe lo que se observa desde fuera.
explanation.pt-BR: Radical de adjetivo い (ou な-adjetivo + そう) + そうに descreve a aparência: 残念そうに 'com ar de pena', 嬉しそうに 'parecendo feliz'. Descreve sempre o que se vê de fora.

name: 〜そうになる (about to; on the verge of)

explanation.en: Verb stem + そうになる expresses being on the verge of something happening, often unintentionally. It indicates that something almost happened or is about to happen. In the song: 負けそうになる = 'about to lose / on the verge of losing.'
explanation.es: Raiz del verbo + そうになる expresa estar a punto de que algo suceda, a menudo involuntariamente. En la cancion: 負けそうになる = 'a punto de perder / al borde de perder.'
explanation.pt-BR: Radical do verbo + そうになる expressa estar a ponto de algo acontecer, muitas vezes involuntariamente. Na musica: 負けそうになる = 'prestes a perder / a beira de perder.'

explanation.en:
How it works: たくない (takunai) is the negative of たい (tai, 'want to'). Take the verb stem, add たい, then conjugate it like an i-adjective: たい → たくない.

Example from this song: 帰りたくない (kaeritakunai) = 'don't want to go home' — from 帰る (kaeru, 'to go home') → 帰り (kaeri, stem) + たい (tai) → 帰りたくない (kaeritakunai)

More examples:
• 食べたくない (tabetakunai, 'don't want to eat') — from 食べる (taberu, 'to eat')
• 起きたくない (okitakunai, 'don't want to get up') — from 起きる (okiru, 'to wake up')
• 会いたくない (aitakunai, 'don't want to meet') — from 会う (au, 'to meet')

Note: たい conjugates like an i-adjective: たい → たくない (negative) → たかった (past) → たくなかった (past negative). This makes it very versatile for expressing desires.

How it works: Take the たい (tai, 'want to') form of a verb, change い to く, then add なる (naru, 'to become'). This expresses a spontaneous feeling arising — 'come to want to do X'.

Example from this song: 泣きたくなる (nakitaku naru) = 'come to want to cry' — from 泣く (naku, 'to cry') → 泣きたい (nakitai, 'want to cry') → 泣きたく (nakitaku) + なる (naru, 'become') = 泣きたくなる (nakitaku naru)

More examples:
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べたくなる (tabetaku naru, 'come to want to eat')
• 帰る (kaeru, 'to return') → 帰りたくなる (kaeritaku naru, 'come to want to go home')
• 会う (au, 'to meet') → 会いたくなる (aitaku naru, 'come to want to see someone')

Note: This describes feelings that arise naturally, not deliberate decisions. たい conjugates like an い-adjective: たい → たく (adverb form) + なる.

name: 〜たらいいのに (tara ii noni - if only)

explanation.en:
Expresses a wish for something that is unlikely or impossible. "If only [X would happen]..." It carries a feeling of longing or frustration.

How it works:
Take the たら (tara, conditional) form of a verb and add いいのに (ii noni, "it would be nice, but...").

Example from this song:
君の事嫌いになれたらいいのに (kimi no koto kirai ni naretara ii noni, "If only I could grow to dislike you")

More examples:
- 飛べたらいいのに (tobetara ii noni, "If only I could fly")
- もっと時間があったらいいのに (motto jikan ga attara ii noni, "If only there were more time")
- 日本語が上手だったらいいのに (nihongo ga jouzu dattara ii noni, "If only my Japanese were better")

name: 〜たりする (tari suru) — sometimes / among other things

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb た-form (ta-form) + り (ri) + する (suru) means "do things like ~" or "sometimes ~." It lists actions as examples, implying there are others too. You can list multiple: AたりBたりする (A tari B tari suru, "do things like A and B"). It gives a casual, non-exhaustive feeling.

Example from this song:
わからなくなったりする (wakaranaku nattari suru) — "sometimes I become confused"
The singer admits to occasionally losing their way — it happens from time to time.

More examples:
• 週末は映画を見たり買い物したりする (shuumatsu wa eiga o mitari kaimono shitari suru) — "on weekends I do things like watch movies and go shopping"
• 泣いたり笑ったりする (naitari warattari suru) — "sometimes cry, sometimes laugh"
• 忘れたりしないよ (wasuretari shinai yo) — "I won't do things like forgetting (you)"

How it works: だけ (dake, 'only/just') + で (de, 'by/with') after a verb or noun means 'just by doing X' or 'with only X'. It expresses that something minimal is sufficient for a result.

Example from this song: 見てるだけで幸せ (miteru dake de shiawase) = 'just by watching, I'm happy' — 見てる (miteru, 'watching') + だけ (dake, 'just') + で (de, 'by') + 幸せ (shiawase, 'happy')

More examples:
• 話すだけで楽しい (hanasu dake de tanoshii, 'just talking is fun')
• それだけで十分 (sore dake de juubun, 'just that is enough')
• いるだけで安心する (iru dake de anshin suru, 'just being there puts me at ease')

Note: This pattern beautifully expresses that even a small thing brings great feelings — very common in love songs.

How it works: だけ (dake) means 'only' or 'just,' and adding の (no) lets it modify a noun. Together, だけの means 'only for' or 'exclusively belonging to.'

Example from this song: 僕らだけの名前 (bokura dake no namae) = 'a name that belongs only to us' — from 僕ら (bokura, 'we/us') + だけの (dake no) + 名前 (namae, 'name')

More examples:
• 二人だけの秘密 (futari dake no himitsu, 'a secret just between the two of us') — from 二人 (futari, 'two people')
• 自分だけの世界 (jibun dake no sekai, 'a world all your own') — from 自分 (jibun, 'oneself')
• 今日だけの特別 (kyou dake no tokubetsu, 'special for today only') — from 今日 (kyou, 'today')

Note: だけ alone limits quantity ('only X'). だけの modifies the following noun to express exclusivity. It creates a warm, intimate feeling when used with relationships.

How it works: Add だけは (dake wa) after a noun to emphasize 'at least this one thing' — expressing that even if everything else fails, this one thing matters most.

Example from this song: 夢だけは (yume dake wa) = 'at least my dream' — from 夢 (yume, 'dream') + だけは (dake wa, 'at least') — expressing determination to protect this one thing above all.

More examples:
• これ (kore, 'this') → これだけは (kore dake wa, 'at least this')
• 約束 (yakusoku, 'promise') → 約束だけは (yakusoku dake wa, 'at least the promise')
• 言いたいこと (iitai koto, 'what I want to say') → 言いたいことだけは (iitai koto dake wa, 'at least what I want to say')

Note: だけ = 'only'. Adding は after it adds emphasis and contrast — 'as for at least this one thing'. It implies 'everything else may be uncertain, but THIS is certain'.

name: 〜ちゃいけない (cha ikenai: must not)

explanation.en:
How it works: ちゃいけない (cha ikenai) is the casual form of てはいけない (te wa ikenai), meaning 'must not' or 'it's not OK to.' It expresses prohibition.

Example from this song: 忘れちゃいけない (wasureccha ikenai) = 'must not forget' — from 忘れる (wasureru, 'to forget') → 忘れては (wasurete wa) → casual: 忘れちゃ (wasureccha) + いけない (ikenai)

More examples:
• 食べちゃいけない (tabeccha ikenai, 'must not eat') — from 食べる (taberu, 'to eat')
• 言っちゃいけない (iccha ikenai, 'must not say') — from 言う (iu, 'to say')
• 泣いちゃダメ (naiccha dame, 'you mustn't cry') — from 泣く (naku, 'to cry') — ダメ is another way to say 'not allowed'

Note: The contraction pattern: ては → ちゃ, では → じゃ. So 飲んではいけない (nonde wa ikenai) → 飲んじゃいけない (nonjya ikenai, 'must not drink').

How it works: The っと (tto) ending is added to adverbs and mimetic words (onomatopoeia) to emphasize the manner or feeling of an action. The small っ adds a sharp, crisp quality.

Example from this song: The song uses words like そっと (sotto, 'gently/quietly') and ギュッと (gyutto, 'tightly/squeezing') — mimetic adverbs with っと that vividly describe how actions are performed.

More examples:
• じっと (jitto, 'still/staring intently')
• ぐっと (gutto, 'with force / holding back emotions')
• パッと (patto, 'suddenly/brightly')
• ふわっと (fuwatto, 'softly/floatily')

Note: Japanese has a rich system of mimetic words (擬態語, gitaigo). The っと pattern makes them feel more immediate and vivid. These words are essential for natural-sounding Japanese and are very common in everyday speech.

name: 〜ていける (te ikeru) — can keep doing / can go on

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb て-form (te-form) + いける (ikeru) means "can keep doing ~" or "can go on doing ~." It combines ていく (te iku, progressive into the future) with the potential form いける (ikeru, "can go"). It expresses confidence that something can be sustained or continued.

Example from this song:
変えていける (kaete ikeru) — "can keep changing"
The singer believes they have the power to continue transforming things.

More examples:
• 一人でもやっていける (hitori demo yatte ikeru) — "I can manage even alone"
• この調子で続けていける (kono choushi de tsuzukete ikeru) — "can keep going at this pace"
• 二人なら乗り越えていける (futari nara norikoete ikeru) — "together we can keep overcoming"

name: 〜ていった (went on doing / faded away)

explanation.en:
How it works: Combine a verb's te-form with いった (itta, past of いく) to express an action that moved away or progressed over time in the past. It shows something gradually happening and going away.

Example from this song: 消えていった (kiete itta) = 'faded away / disappeared gradually' — from 消える (kieru, 'to disappear') → 消えて (kiete) + いった (itta)

More examples:
• 走っていった (hashitte itta, 'ran off/away') — from 走る (hashiru, 'to run')
• 変わっていった (kawatte itta, 'gradually changed over time') — from 変わる (kawaru, 'to change')
• 忘れていった (wasurete itta, 'gradually forgot') — from 忘れる (wasureru, 'to forget')

Note: ていく (te iku) = going forward from now. ていった (te itta) = went forward in the past. The emphasis is on movement away from the speaker or progression through time.

name: 〜ていますか (te imasu ka - are you doing?)

explanation.en:
A polite progressive question asking whether someone is currently doing something or in an ongoing state.

How it works:
Take the て-form (te-form) of a verb, add います (imasu, polite "to be"), then か (ka, question particle).

Example from this song:
君は覚えていますか (kimi wa oboete imasu ka, "Do you remember?")

More examples:
- 今何をしていますか (ima nani o shite imasu ka, "What are you doing now?")
- 日本語を勉強していますか (nihongo o benkyou shite imasu ka, "Are you studying Japanese?")
- まだ待っていますか (mada matte imasu ka, "Are you still waiting?")

How it works: Combine the て-form + いく (iku, 'to go') + ぜ (ze, masculine emphasis particle). This creates an energetic, masculine declaration — 'I'm gonna keep doing it!' The いく often contracts away.

Example from this song: The song uses this pattern to express determined forward momentum with a rough, energetic masculine tone.

More examples:
• 行く (iku, 'to go') → 行ってくぜ (ittekuze, 'I'm heading out!')
• やる (yaru, 'to do') → やってくぜ (yattekuze, 'I'm gonna do it!')
• 走る (hashiru, 'to run') → 走ってくぜ (hashittekuze, 'I'm gonna run!')

Note: ぜ (ze) is a rough masculine sentence-ending particle that adds energy and assertion. It's less aggressive than ぞ (zo). Common in shonen anime and J-rock. Think Naruto saying 行くってばよ (ikuttebayo) — similarly energetic but different particle.

〜ていた contracts to 〜てた in casual speech and lyrics — describing an ongoing past state or action. 重なってた 'was overlapping', 強がってた 'was acting tough', 見守ってた 'was watching over'. Drop the い for the casual form.
explanation.es: 〜ていた se contrae a 〜てた en el habla casual y en letras — describe estado o acción continuos en pasado. 重なってた 'se estaba superponiendo', 強がってた 'me hacía el fuerte'. Cae la い en la forma casual.
explanation.pt-BR: 〜ていた contrai para 〜てた no falar casual e em letras — descreve estado ou ação contínuos no passado. 重なってた 'estava se sobrepondo', 強がってた 'estava bancando o forte'. Cai o い na forma casual.

name: 〜てみたい (te mitai) — want to try doing

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb て-form (te-form) + みたい (mitai) combines two patterns: てみる (te miru, "to try doing ~") and たい (tai, "want to ~"). Together, てみたい (te mitai) means "I want to try doing ~." It expresses curiosity and the desire to experience something new.

Example from this song:
The singer expresses wanting to try new experiences — to step into the unknown.

More examples:
• 日本料理を作ってみたい (nihon ryouri o tsukutte mitai) — "I want to try making Japanese food"
• スカイダイビングをしてみたい (sukaidaibingu o shite mitai) — "I want to try skydiving"
• この本を読んでみたい (kono hon o yonde mitai) — "I want to try reading this book"

name: 〜てもいい (temo ii - it’s okay to)

explanation.en:
Expresses permission or willingness: "it’s okay to [do X]" or "I don’t mind if [X]." The speaker accepts the action described.

How it works:
Take the て-form (te-form) of a verb and add もいい (mo ii).

Example from this song:
すべてを犠牲にしてもいい (subete o gisei ni shite mo ii, "It’s fine to sacrifice everything")

More examples:
- ここに座ってもいいですか (koko ni suwatte mo ii desu ka, "May I sit here?")
- 食べてもいいよ (tabete mo ii yo, "You can eat it")
- 遅れてもいいから来て (okurete mo ii kara kite, "It’s okay to be late, just come")

How it works: てん (ten) is an ultra-casual spoken contraction of ている (te iru, 'is doing'). The いる gets compressed: ている → てる → てん. This is common in song lyrics and very informal speech.

Example from this song: はえてん (haeten) = 'have (wings)' — from はえている (haete iru, 'wings are growing') → はえてる (haeteru) → はえてん (haeten)

More examples:
• 知ってん (shitten, 'I know') — from 知っている (shitte iru)
• 食べてん (tabeten, 'am eating') — from 食べている (tabete iru)
• 待ってん (matten, 'am waiting') — from 待っている (matte iru)

Note: This contraction is regional (common in Kansai dialect) and very casual. The standard casual contraction is てる (teru). てん (ten) is one step more casual and is frequently heard in song lyrics.

name: 〜であろう (de arou - probably is/will be)

explanation.en:
A formal way to express conjecture or probability, similar to "will probably be" or "is likely." This is the volitional form of である (de aru), which is the formal equivalent of だ (da). You will encounter it in literature, formal speeches, and dramatic lyrics.

How it works:
Place であろう (de arou) after a noun or na-adjective stem. It replaces だろう (darou) in formal/literary registers.

Example from this song:
これから先訪れるであろう全てを (korekara saki otozureru de arou subete o, "Everything that will likely come from here on")

More examples:
- 困難であろう (konnan de arou, "it will probably be difficult")
- 彼は天才であろう (kare wa tensai de arou, "he is probably a genius")
- 正しいであろう判断 (tadashii de arou handan, "a judgment that is probably correct")

How it works: Use noun + であろうと (de arou to) to express 'whether it be X (or Y)'. It's a formal conditional showing indifference to conditions — the result holds regardless.

Example from this song: 架空であろうと現実だろうと (kakuu de arou to genjitsu darou to) = 'whether it be fiction or reality' — expressing that it doesn't matter which one it is.

More examples:
• 雨 (ame, 'rain') → 雨であろうと (ame de arou to, 'whether it be rain')
• 誰 (dare, 'who') → 誰であろうと (dare de arou to, 'whoever it may be')
• 何 (nani, 'what') → 何であろうと (nani de arou to, 'whatever it may be')

Note: であろうと is the formal equivalent of でも (demo). It's used in literary, poetic, or dramatic contexts. The pattern A であろうと B であろうと means 'whether A or B'.

How it works: Use で (de, state marker) + いて (ite, te-form of いる, 'to be') to request someone to remain in a certain state — 'please stay/be [adjective]'. Often used with adjectives and な-adjectives.

Example from this song: The song asks someone to stay a certain way — 'please remain as you are' — using でいて to express the wish for continued existence in that state.

More examples:
• 元気 (genki, 'healthy') → 元気でいて (genki de ite, 'please stay healthy')
• そのまま (sono mama, 'as is') → そのままでいて (sono mama de ite, 'please stay as you are')
• 優しい (yasashii, 'kind') → 優しくいて (yasashiku ite, 'please stay kind')

Note: For な-adjectives and nouns, use で: 元気でいて. For い-adjectives, use the く-form: 優しくいて. Adding ください makes it more polite: 元気でいてください.

name: 〜でしかない (de shika nai: can only be)

explanation.en:
How it works: Use noun + でしかない (de shika nai) to express limitation — 'can only be X' or 'nothing more than X'. しか always pairs with a negative.

Example from this song: 僕でしかない (boku de shika nai) = 'can only be me / I'm nothing more than myself' — from 僕 (boku, 'I') + で (de) + しか (shika, 'only') + ない (nai, 'not')

More examples:
• 夢 (yume, 'dream') → 夢でしかない (yume de shika nai, 'it's nothing but a dream')
• 始まり (hajimari, 'beginning') → 始まりでしかない (hajimari de shika nai, 'it's only the beginning')
• 人間 (ningen, 'human') → 人間でしかない (ningen de shika nai, 'merely human')

Note: でしかない expresses humble limitation — accepting what you are or what something is. It can be self-deprecating or philosophical depending on context.

How it works: Add でしょ (desho) at the end of a statement to seek confirmation or express assumption — 'right?' or 'isn't it?'. It's the casual form of でしょう (deshou).

Example from this song: 覚悟でしょ (kakugo desho) = 'you're prepared, right?' — from 覚悟 (kakugo, 'readiness/resolve') + でしょ (desho, 'right?')

More examples:
• 分かる (wakaru, 'to understand') → 分かるでしょ (wakaru desho, 'you understand, right?')
• 寒い (samui, 'cold') → 寒いでしょ (samui desho, 'it's cold, right?')
• 本当 (hontou, 'true') → 本当でしょ (hontou desho, 'it's true, right?')

Note: With rising intonation, でしょ seeks confirmation. With falling intonation, it asserts 'I told you so'. でしょう (long form) is more polite; でしょ (short) is casual.

name: 〜というの (to iu no) — are you saying that / the fact that

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Clause + というの (to iu no) means "are you saying that ~?" (questioning) or "the fact that ~" (nominalizing). It wraps an entire statement into something that can be questioned or discussed. In questions, it often carries surprise or disbelief.

Example from this song:
行くというの (iku to iu no) — "are you saying you'll go?" / "you're going, you say?"
The singer questions someone's claim with surprise or disbelief.

More examples:
• 知らないというの？ (shiranai to iu no?) — "are you saying you don't know?"
• 嘘だというのか (uso da to iu no ka) — "are you saying it's a lie?"
• 彼が来るというのは本当？ (kare ga kuru to iu no wa hontou?) — "is it true that he's coming?"

name: 〜とか〜とか (toka ... toka) — things like ~ and ~

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern X + とか (toka) + Y + とか (toka) lists examples casually — "things like X and Y." It implies there are other items too, but you are just mentioning a few. It is more casual than や (ya) and very common in everyday speech. You can list verbs, nouns, or even sentences.

Example from this song:
The singer casually lists different experiences or feelings as examples of what they go through.

More examples:
• サッカーとかバスケとか好き (sakkaa toka basuke toka suki) — "I like things like soccer and basketball"
• 映画を見るとか本を読むとか (eiga o miru toka hon o yomu toka) — "things like watching movies and reading books"
• 東京とか大阪とかに行きたい (toukyou toka oosaka toka ni ikitai) — "I want to go to places like Tokyo and Osaka"

How it works: Add として (toshite) after a noun to mean 'as (a role/capacity)' or to set up a hypothetical frame. It establishes the perspective or role through which something is considered.

Example from this song: The song uses として to frame scenarios hypothetically — 'assuming this is the case' or 'as if this were so'.

More examples:
• 先生 (sensei, 'teacher') → 先生として (sensei toshite, 'as a teacher')
• 友達 (tomodachi, 'friend') → 友達として (tomodachi toshite, 'as a friend')
• 日本人 (nihonjin, 'Japanese person') → 日本人として (nihonjin toshite, 'as a Japanese person')

Note: として can also mean 'even (one)' in negative sentences: 一人として来なかった (hitori toshite konakatta, 'not even one person came').

How it works: Use noun + と (to) + なる (naru, 'to become') to express transformation — something becomes something else. と marks what it transforms into.

Example from this song: 勇気となる (yuuki to naru) = 'becomes courage' — from 勇気 (yuuki, 'courage') + と (to, 'into') + なる (naru, 'to become')

More examples:
• 力 (chikara, 'strength') → 力となる (chikara to naru, 'becomes strength')
• 光 (hikari, 'light') → 光となる (hikari to naru, 'becomes light')
• 問題 (mondai, 'problem') → 問題となる (mondai to naru, 'becomes a problem')

Note: となる is slightly more formal/literary than になる (ni naru). Both mean 'become', but となる often implies a more significant or dramatic transformation. In songs and literature, となる adds weight.

How it works: と (to) is the quotation particle. Place it after what someone said or thought, followed by 言う (iu, 'to say') or other verbs of expression.

Example from this song: ピエロになると言って (piero ni naru to itte) = 'saying "I'll become a clown"' — from ピエロになる (piero ni naru, 'to become a clown') + と (to) + 言って (itte, te-form of 言う)

More examples:
• 好きだと言った (suki da to itta, 'said "I like you"') — from 好き (suki, 'like')
• 行くと思う (iku to omou, 'I think I'll go') — with 思う (omou, 'to think')
• 大丈夫だと聞いた (daijoubu da to kiita, 'I heard it's OK') — with 聞く (kiku, 'to hear')

Note: と quotes both direct and indirect speech. The quoted part uses plain form. Common verbs after と: 言う (iu, say), 思う (omou, think), 聞く (kiku, hear), 書く (kaku, write).

How it works: Add な (na) after the dictionary form of a verb to create a negative command — 'Don't do X!'

Example from this song: まけるな (makeru na) = 'Don't lose!' — from まける (makeru, 'to lose') + な (na, prohibition)

More examples:
• 泣く (naku, 'to cry') → 泣くな (naku na, 'Don't cry!')
• 止まる (tomaru, 'to stop') → 止まるな (tomaru na, 'Don't stop!')
• あきらめる (akirameru, 'to give up') → あきらめるな (akirameru na, 'Don't give up!')

Note: This is the opposite of the imperative — instead of ordering action, it forbids it. Very common in sports and battle anime. Dictionary form + な = prohibition.

name: 〜ないでいる (naide iru: to remain not doing)

explanation.en:
How it works: Use the negative て-form ないで (naide, 'without doing') + いる (iru, 'to be') to express deliberately maintaining a state of NOT doing something — 'to remain without doing X'.

Example from this song: 変わらないでいよう (kawaranaide iyou) = 'let's stay unchanged / let's remain as we are' — from 変わる (kawaru, 'to change') → 変わらないで (kawaranaide, 'without changing') + いよう (iyou, volitional of いる, 'let's be')

More examples:
• 忘れる (wasureru, 'to forget') → 忘れないでいる (wasurenaide iru, 'to remain not forgetting')
• 泣く (naku, 'to cry') → 泣かないでいる (nakanaide iru, 'to hold back tears')
• 言う (iu, 'to say') → 言わないでいる (iwanaide iru, 'to keep not saying it')

Note: This pattern implies a conscious choice to maintain a state. 変わらないでいよう is a beautiful wish — choosing together to stay as you are. The volitional いよう makes it an invitation.

name: 〜ないように / 〜ように (you ni: so (not) to)

explanation.en:
Attach after a verb to express a purpose or desired outcome. 〜ないように = 'so as not to'; 〜ように = 'so that / like'.

From this song: こわれないように = 'so as not to break'.

More examples:
• 風邪を引かないように (so as not to catch a cold)
• 遅れないように気をつける (be careful not to be late)
• 分かるように話す (explain so it's understandable)

name: 〜なかった (nakatta - could not / did not)

explanation.en:
The past negative form of verbs, meaning "could not" or "did not." One of the most fundamental conjugations in Japanese.

How it works:
Take the ない-form (nai-form) of a verb, replace ない (nai) with なかった (nakatta).

Example from this song:
果たせなかった約束 (hatasenakatta yakusoku, "Promises we could not fulfill")

More examples:
- 行けなかった (ikenakatta, "could not go")
- 食べなかった (tabenakatta, "did not eat")
- 間に合わなかった (ma ni awanakatta, "did not make it in time")

Verb stem + ながら = 'while V-ing.' Two main uses: (1) SIMULTANEOUS — two actions same subject, one in parallel (歩きながら歌う 'sing while walking'); (2) CONCESSIVE — 'even while V-ing' / 'despite' (躓きながらでも 'even while stumbling'). Sense (2) is often clarified with でも following: 躓きながらでも = 'even while stumbling.' Brave Soul uses both — 迷いながら ('while wandering') is sense (1); 躓きながらでも ('even while stumbling') is sense (2).
explanation.es: Raíz del verbo + ながら = 'mientras V'. Dos usos principales: (1) SIMULTÁNEO — dos acciones, mismo sujeto, en paralelo (歩きながら歌う 'cantar mientras camina'); (2) CONCESIVO — 'aun mientras V' / 'a pesar de' (躓きながらでも 'aunque tropiece'). Sentido (2) suele clarificarse con でも después. Brave Soul usa ambos — 迷いながら ('mientras se pierde') es (1); 躓きながらでも ('aunque tropiece') es (2).
explanation.pt-BR: Raiz do verbo + ながら = 'enquanto V'. Dois usos principais: (1) SIMULTÂNEO — duas ações, mesmo sujeito, em paralelo (歩きながら歌う 'cantar enquanto caminha'); (2) CONCESSIVO — 'mesmo enquanto V' / 'apesar de' (躓きながらでも 'mesmo tropeçando'). Sentido (2) frequentemente esclarecido por でも depois. Brave Soul usa os dois — 迷いながら ('enquanto se perde') é (1); 躓きながらでも ('mesmo tropeçando') é (2).

explanation.en:
How it works: ながらも (nagara mo) adds も (mo, 'even') to ながら (nagara, 'while') to express doing two contradictory or contrasting things simultaneously. It emphasizes the contrast between them.

Example from this song: 明け暮れながらも (akekure nagara mo) = 'even while spending days (in that state)' — from 明け暮れる (akekureru, 'to spend one's days')

More examples:
• 知りながらも黙っていた (shiri nagara mo damatte ita, 'kept quiet even while knowing') — from 知る (shiru, 'to know')
• 小さいながらも頑張る (chiisai nagara mo ganbaru, 'try hard despite being small')
• 泣きながらも笑った (naki nagara mo waratta, 'smiled even while crying') — from 泣く (naku, 'to cry')

Note: Plain ながら means 'while doing X.' Adding も creates a concessive meaning: 'even while/despite X.' This highlights that the two actions seem contradictory.

name: 〜なきゃよかった (nakya yokatta - wish I hadn’t)

explanation.en:
Expresses regret about something that already happened: "I wish I hadn’t [done X]." なきゃ is a casual contraction of なければ (nakereba).

How it works:
Take the ない-form (nai-form) of a verb, contract it to なきゃ (nakya), then add よかった (yokatta, "it would have been better").

Example from this song:
こんな気持ち知らなきゃよかった (konna kimochi shiranakya yokatta, "I wish I’d never known these feelings")

More examples:
- 行かなきゃよかった (ikanakya yokatta, "I wish I hadn’t gone")
- 食べなきゃよかった (tabenakya yokatta, "I wish I hadn’t eaten that")
- 言わなきゃよかった (iwanakya yokatta, "I wish I hadn’t said that")

name: 〜なくちゃいけない (nakucha ikenai: must do)

explanation.en:
How it works: This is a casual contraction of なくてはいけない (nakutewa ikenai). Take the ない-form of a verb, drop い, add くちゃいけない. Literally 'if I don't do it, it won't do' = 'I must do it'.

Example from this song: 謝らなくちゃいけない (ayamaranakucha ikenai) = 'I must apologize' — from 謝る (ayamaru, 'to apologize') → 謝らない (ayamaranai, negative) → 謝らなくちゃいけない

More examples:
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べなくちゃいけない (tabenakucha ikenai, 'must eat')
• 行く (iku, 'to go') → 行かなくちゃいけない (ikanakucha ikenai, 'must go')
• 勉強する (benkyou suru, 'to study') → 勉強しなくちゃいけない (benkyou shinakucha ikenai, 'must study')

Note: Even shorter casual forms exist: なくちゃ (nakucha) or なきゃ (nakya). So 行かなきゃ (ikanakya) = 'gotta go'.

name: 〜なくてもいい (don't have to; it's okay not to)

explanation.en:
How it works: Take the negative form of a verb or adjective, change ない to なくても, and add いい (ii, 'good'). This means 'you don't have to' or 'it's OK not to.'

Example from this song: 強くなくてもいい (tsuyoku nakutemo ii) = 'it's okay not to be strong' — from 強い (tsuyoi, 'strong') → 強くない (tsuyoku nai) → 強くなくてもいい

More examples:
• 行かなくてもいい (ikanakutemo ii, 'you don't have to go') — from 行く (iku, 'to go')
• 完璧じゃなくてもいい (kanpeki ja nakutemo ii, 'it doesn't have to be perfect')
• 急がなくてもいい (isoganakutemo ii, 'you don't need to hurry') — from 急ぐ (isogu, 'to hurry')

Note: This is the opposite of なければならない (nakereba naranai, 'must do'). It gives permission NOT to do something, which can be very comforting.

How it works: なけりゃ (nakerya) is the casual spoken contraction of なければ (nakereba), meaning 'if not.' It's common in songs, anime, and informal speech.

Example from this song: The song uses なけりゃ as a casual 'if not' — expressing what needs to happen or what would go wrong without something.

More examples:
• 行かなけりゃ (ikanakerya, 'if I don't go') — from 行く (iku, 'to go')
• やらなけりゃダメだ (yaranakerya dame da, 'you gotta do it') — from やる (yaru, 'to do')
• 食べなけりゃ死ぬ (tabenakerya shinu, 'if you don't eat, you'll die')

Note: Contraction chain: なければ → なけりゃ → なきゃ. なきゃ is even more casual. All three mean 'if not' / 'must.' なけりゃならない = 'must do' (casual of なければならない).

How it works: な (na) after a verb's dictionary form is a casual negative command: 'don't do X!' Adding よ (yo) makes it slightly softer or more emphatic depending on tone.

Example from this song: 隠すなよ (kakusu na yo) = 'don't hide it!' — from 隠す (kakusu, 'to hide') + な (na, 'don't') + よ (yo)

More examples:
• 泣くな (naku na, 'don't cry!') — from 泣く (naku, 'to cry')
• 心配するなよ (shinpai suru na yo, 'don't worry!') — from 心配する (shinpai suru, 'to worry')
• 諦めるな (akirameru na, 'don't give up!') — from 諦める (akirameru, 'to give up')

Note: Dictionary form + な is the rough masculine prohibition form. It's very common in anime and songs. Don't confuse with the な that makes na-adjectives (静かな = quiet).

name: 〜なりに (nari ni: in one's own way)

explanation.en:
How it works: Add なりに (nari ni) after a noun or pronoun to express 'in one's own way' or 'to the best of one's ability' — doing something within one's own capacity or style.

Example from this song: 私なりに (watashi nari ni) = 'in my own way' — from 私 (watashi, 'I/me') + なりに (nari ni, 'in one's own way')

More examples:
• 自分 (jibun, 'oneself') → 自分なりに (jibun nari ni, 'in my own way')
• 子供 (kodomo, 'child') → 子供なりに (kodomo nari ni, 'in a child's own way')
• 彼 (kare, 'he') → 彼なりに (kare nari ni, 'in his own way')

Note: なりに implies doing the best you can with what you have. 子供なりに頑張った (kodomo nari ni ganbatta, 'tried hard in a child's own way') acknowledges effort within limitations. It's humble and genuine.

How it works: Use noun + にしか (ni shika, 'only to') + negative verb to restrict meaning — 'can only [verb] to/for [noun]'. しか always needs a negative.

Example from this song: 僕にしか見れない (boku ni shika mirenai) = 'that only I can see' — from 僕 (boku, 'I') + にしか (ni shika, 'only to') + 見れない (mirenai, 'can't see')

More examples:
• 君 (kimi, 'you') → 君にしかできない (kimi ni shika dekinai, 'only you can do it')
• ここ (koko, 'here') → ここにしかない (koko ni shika nai, 'only exists here')
• 今 (ima, 'now') → 今しかない (ima shika nai, 'it's now or never')

Note: にしか emphasizes exclusivity with an emotional weight — it's not just 'only' but 'ONLY this and nothing else'. In this song, it's empowering: something unique to 'me' that no one else can see.
Noun (or な-adjective) + にする means 'make/turn into X' — actively transform something. 声をfreeに(する) 'make the voice free'; クリーンにする 'make clean'. Distinct from 〜になる ('become X' — intransitive).
explanation.es: Sustantivo (o な-adjetivo) + にする significa 'convertir en X' — acción activa. 声をfreeに(する) 'liberar la voz'; クリーンにする 'volver limpio'. Distinto de 〜になる ('volverse X' — intransitivo).
explanation.pt-BR: Substantivo (ou な-adjetivo) + にする significa 'transformar em X' — ação ativa. 声をfreeに(する) 'libertar a voz'; クリーンにする 'tornar limpo'. Diferente de 〜になる ('tornar-se X' — intransitivo).

explanation.en:
How it works: にだって (ni datte) combines に (ni, 'by') with だって (datte, 'even'). It emphasizes that even the stated agent or means can or can't do something.

Example from this song: テロリストにだって消せない (terorisuto ni datte kesenai) = 'even a terrorist can't erase it' — emphasizing that not even the most extreme agent can destroy it

More examples:
• 誰にだって秘密がある (dare ni datte himitsu ga aru, 'even anyone has secrets / everyone has secrets')
• 子供にだってわかる (kodomo ni datte wakaru, 'even a child can understand')
• 親にだって言えない (oya ni datte ienai, 'can't tell even my parents')

Note: だって adds the nuance of 'even.' It's more emphatic than でも. にだって specifically emphasizes 'even by (this agent).' It's a punk/rebellious way to make a strong point.

How it works: Combine に (ni, 'into') + でも (demo, 'even') + なれる (nareru, 'can become') to express willingness to become something, even something extreme. It shows determination or desperation.

Example from this song: The song expresses the intensity of being willing to become anything — 'I can even become [something extreme]' — showing the singer's resolve.

More examples:
• 鬼 (oni, 'demon') → 鬼にでもなれる (oni ni demo nareru, 'can even become a demon')
• 何 (nani, 'anything') → 何にでもなれる (nani ni demo nareru, 'can become anything')
• 盾 (tate, 'shield') → 盾にでもなれる (tate ni demo nareru, 'can even become a shield')

Note: でも adds the nuance of 'even' — it emphasizes that the subject is willing to go to that extreme. Without でも, it's simply 'can become'. なれる is the potential form of なる (naru, 'to become').

name: 〜にも...ない (not even / no one can)

explanation.en:
How it works: Combine a question word (誰/dare = who, 何/nani = what, どこ/doko = where) with にも (ni mo) and a negative verb. This creates absolute negation — 'no one', 'nothing', 'nowhere'.

Example from this song: 誰にも見れない (dare ni mo mirenai) = 'no one can see' — from 誰 (dare, 'who') + にも (ni mo, 'even to') + 見れない (mirenai, 'cannot see')

More examples:
• 何も食べない (nani mo tabenai, 'eat nothing / don't eat anything')
• どこにも行かない (doko ni mo ikanai, 'don't go anywhere')
• 誰にも言わない (dare ni mo iwanai, 'won't tell anyone')

Note: The particle も (mo) combined with a negative verb creates total negation. Without the negative, も means 'also/even'. 誰にも (dare ni mo) + positive = 'to everyone'; + negative = 'to no one'.

name: 〜にも負けず (ni mo makezu) — without losing to / undaunted by

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Noun + にも (ni mo) + 負けず (makezu) means "without losing to ~" or "undaunted by ~." 負ける (makeru) means "to lose," and 負けず (makezu) is its classical negative form (ず = without). This expression is famous from Miyazawa Kenji's poem "Ame ni mo Makezu" ("Not losing to the rain"). It conveys endurance and resilience.

Example from this song:
雨にも負けず (ame ni mo makezu) — "not losing to the rain"
A declaration of perseverance against all natural forces and hardships.

More examples:
• 風にも負けず (kaze ni mo makezu) — "not losing to the wind"
• 困難にも負けず前に進む (konnan ni mo makezu mae ni susumu) — "moving forward without losing to difficulties"
• 病気にも負けず頑張った (byouki ni mo makezu ganbatta) — "persevered without losing to illness"

How it works: Use noun + に (ni, 'into') + 変わる (kawaru, 'to change') to express transformation from one thing to another. The particle に marks what something changes into.

Example from this song: 声が耳鳴りに変わった (koe ga miminari ni kawatta) = 'the voice changed into a ringing in the ears' — from 声 (koe, 'voice') + が (ga, subject) + 耳鳴り (miminari, 'ringing') + に (ni, 'into') + 変わった (kawatta, 'changed')

More examples:
• 雨が雪に変わる (ame ga yuki ni kawaru, 'the rain changes to snow')
• 緑が赤に変わる (midori ga aka ni kawaru, 'green changes to red')
• 笑顔が涙に変わった (egao ga namida ni kawatta, 'the smile turned to tears')

Note: 変わる (kawaru) is intransitive (changes by itself). 変える (kaeru) is transitive (someone changes it). 色を変える (iro wo kaeru, 'to change the color').

How it works:
The pattern Verb ます-stem (masu-stem) + に来る (ni kuru) means "to come in order to do ~." It expresses purpose of movement — someone comes with the specific intention of performing an action. Past tense: に来た (ni kita, "came to do").

Example from this song:
伝えに来た (tsutae ni kita) — "came to tell (you)"
The singer traveled specifically to deliver a message.

More examples:
• 遊びに来て (asobi ni kite) — "come hang out" / "come visit"
• 日本語を勉強しに来た (nihongo o benkyou shi ni kita) — "came to study Japanese"
• 助けに来たよ (tasuke ni kita yo) — "I came to help!"

name: 〜ぬように (nu you ni: so as not to)

explanation.en:
How it works: ぬ (nu) is the classical/literary negative form (equivalent to ない), and ように (you ni) means 'so that.' Together, ぬように means 'so as not to' — expressing purpose of prevention.

Example from this song: 色褪せぬように (iroasenu you ni) = 'so that it won't fade' — from 色褪せる (iroaseru, 'to fade in color') → 色褪せ (iroase, stem) + ぬ (nu, negative) + ように (you ni)

More examples:
• 忘れぬように (wasurenu you ni, 'so as not to forget') — from 忘れる (wasureru, 'to forget')
• 消えぬように (kienu you ni, 'so that it won't disappear') — from 消える (kieru, 'to disappear')
• 朽ちぬように (kuchinu you ni, 'so it won't decay') — from 朽ちる (kuchiru, 'to decay')

Note: ぬ is the literary equivalent of ない. It's common in songs, poetry, and formal writing. Modern equivalent: 色褪せないように (iroasenai you ni). ぬ gives a more elegant, timeless feeling.

How it works: Add のか (no ka) at the end of a sentence to create an emotionally charged question, often rhetorical. の adds an explanatory tone, and か marks the question. Together they express doubt, frustration, or deep wondering.

Example from this song: The song uses のか to question reality with emotional weight — 'Is it really...?' or 'Can it be that...?'

More examples:
• 何 (nani, 'what') → 何なのか (nan na no ka, 'what is it, really?')
• できる (dekiru, 'can do') → できるのか (dekiru no ka, 'can it really be done?')
• 本当 (hontō, 'true') → 本当なのか (hontō na no ka, 'is it really true?')

Note: In casual male speech, のか often drops to のか without rising intonation, making it sound reflective rather than questioning. It adds more emotional weight than plain か alone.

How it works:
The pattern Verb/Adjective plain form + のかな (no kana) expresses casual wondering — "I wonder if ~." The の (no) adds explanatory nuance, and かな (kana) expresses uncertainty or self-directed questioning. It is softer and more reflective than a direct question. Very common in song lyrics and inner monologue.

Example from this song:
今もあるのかな (ima mo aru no kana) — "I wonder if it's still there"
The singer gently wonders whether something from the past still exists.

More examples:
• 元気にしてるのかな (genki ni shiteru no kana) — "I wonder if they're doing well"
• これで良かったのかな (kore de yokatta no kana) — "I wonder if this was the right thing"
• 覚えてるのかな (oboeteru no kana) — "I wonder if they remember"
の nominalises + さ adds a casual, confident tone (often male/shounen). 'I'm just going to find it, you know.' Used through this song to give the protagonist a self-assured swagger.
explanation.es: の nominaliza + さ añade un tono casual y seguro (frecuentemente masculino/shounen). Da al protagonista un aire de seguridad despreocupada.
explanation.pt-BR: の nominaliza + さ adiciona um tom casual e confiante (frequentemente masculino/shounen). Dá ao protagonista um ar de autoconfiança displicente.

explanation.en:
How it works: のせい (no sei) means 'because of' or 'due to,' specifically when attributing blame or a negative cause. It implies the cause is at fault.

Example from this song: The song uses のせい to blame something for a negative outcome — 'it's because of (something bad).'

More examples:
• 雨のせいで遅れた (ame no sei de okureta, 'was late because of the rain') — from 雨 (ame, 'rain')
• 君のせいだ (kimi no sei da, 'it's your fault') — from 君 (kimi, 'you')
• 寝不足のせいで (nebusoku no sei de, 'because of lack of sleep')

Note: のせい is for negative causes (blame). For positive causes, use おかげで (okage de, 'thanks to'). 君のせいで泣いた (your fault I cried) vs. 君のおかげで笑えた (thanks to you I could smile).

How it works: Place のならば (no naraba) after a verb to express a formal conditional — 'if it is the case that...'. This is a more formal/literary version of のなら (no nara).

Example from this song: 願うのならば (negau no naraba) = 'if you wish' — from 願う (negau, 'to wish') + のならば (no naraba, 'if it is that')

More examples:
• 行く (iku, 'to go') → 行くのならば (iku no naraba, 'if you are going')
• 戦う (tatakau, 'to fight') → 戦うのならば (tatakau no naraba, 'if you are to fight')
• 信じる (shinjiru, 'to believe') → 信じるのならば (shinjiru no naraba, 'if you believe')

Note: Formality scale: なら (casual) < のなら (standard) < のならば (formal/literary). ならば adds gravitas, making it common in epic anime songs and dramatic speeches.

How it works: のまま (no mama) after a noun means 'remaining as (noun)' or 'while still being (noun).' The state doesn't change.

Example from this song: 自分のまま (jibun no mama) = 'as yourself / remaining true to yourself' — from 自分 (jibun, 'oneself') + のまま (no mama)

More examples:
• 子供のまま (kodomo no mama, 'still a child / remaining childlike') — from 子供 (kodomo, 'child')
• ありのまま (ari no mama, 'as things are / the way it is') — very famous phrase
• 笑顔のまま (egao no mama, 'with a smile still on') — from 笑顔 (egao, 'smile')

Note: ありのまま (ari no mama) is a beloved Japanese phrase meaning 'as you are' — it was famously used as the Japanese title of 'Let It Go.' のまま implies accepting something in its natural, unchanged state.

name: 〜のままに (no mama ni: as it is; following)

explanation.en:
How it works: Use noun + のままに (no mama ni) to express following something without resistance — 'as X dictates' or 'following the flow of X'. まま means 'as is' and に indicates manner.

Example from this song: 衝動のままに (shoudou no mama ni) = 'following the impulse / as the impulse dictates' — from 衝動 (shoudou, 'impulse') + の (no) + ままに (mama ni, 'as is')

More examples:
• 心 (kokoro, 'heart') → 心のままに (kokoro no mama ni, 'following your heart')
• 気持ち (kimochi, 'feeling') → 気持ちのままに (kimochi no mama ni, 'as your feelings dictate')
• 流れ (nagare, 'flow') → 流れのままに (nagare no mama ni, 'going with the flow')

Note: ままに implies surrendering control and letting something guide you. Without に, まま means the state remains unchanged: そのまま (sono mama, 'as it is').

How it works: Place のよう (no you) after a noun to create a simile — 'like X' or 'similar to X'. It can be followed by に (ni) for adverbial use or な (na) to modify nouns.

Example from this song: 雲のよう (kumo no you) = 'like a cloud' — from 雲 (kumo, 'cloud') + のよう (no you, 'like')

More examples:
• 夢 (yume, 'dream') → 夢のような (yume no you na, 'dream-like')
• 子供 (kodomo, 'child') → 子供のように (kodomo no you ni, 'like a child')
• 花 (hana, 'flower') → 花のように美しい (hana no you ni utsukushii, 'beautiful like a flower')

Note: のよう + な = modifies a noun (夢のような話, 'a dream-like story'). のよう + に = modifies a verb (鳥のように飛ぶ, 'fly like a bird'). みたい (mitai) is the casual equivalent.

name: 〜のようで (no you de) — it seems like / is like

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Noun + のようで (no you de) means "it seems like ~" or "it's like ~" and is used to describe something by comparison. The で (de) here is the て-form of だ (da), allowing you to connect this comparison to another clause. It is a softer, more descriptive version of のように (no you ni).

Example from this song:
The singer describes their experience by comparing it to familiar things — making abstract feelings concrete.

More examples:
• 夢のようで信じられない (yume no you de shinjirarenai) — "it's like a dream and I can't believe it"
• 映画のようで面白かった (eiga no you de omoshirokatta) — "it was like a movie and was interesting"
• 嵐のようで激しかった (arashi no you de hageshikatta) — "it was like a storm and was intense"

Comparative structure: noun + のような = 'a [noun] like [the comparison thing] / one akin to.' Modifies the following noun. 名残のような温もり ('warmth akin to a lingering trace'). Compare with 〜のように (adverbial 'in the manner of'): のような modifies a noun, のように modifies a verb / clause. The pair handles all noun-similes in Japanese.
explanation.es: Estructura comparativa: sustantivo + のような = 'un [sustantivo] como [comparación] / parecido a'. Modifica al sustantivo siguiente. 名残のような温もり ('calidez parecida a un vestigio'). Compara con 〜のように (adverbial 'al modo de'): のような modifica sustantivo, のように modifica verbo / cláusula. El par cubre todas las comparaciones con sustantivo en japonés.
explanation.pt-BR: Estrutura comparativa: substantivo + のような = 'um [substantivo] tipo [comparação] / parecido com'. Modifica o substantivo seguinte. 名残のような温もり ('calor parecido com vestígio'). Compare com 〜のように (adverbial 'à maneira de'): のような modifica substantivo, のように modifica verbo / cláusula. O par trata todas as comparações com substantivo no japonês.

name: 〜の方が (no hou ga: the ... one is more)

explanation.en:
How it works: Use A の方が (no hou ga) + adjective to express that A has MORE of that quality. It's the comparison pattern — 'A is more [adj] (than B)'.

Example from this song: 嘘の方がずっと痛かった (uso no hou ga zutto itakatta) = 'the lie was far more painful' — from 嘘 (uso, 'lie') + の方が (no hou ga, 'is more') + ずっと (zutto, 'far more') + 痛かった (itakatta, 'was painful')

More examples:
• こっち (kocchi, 'this one') → こっちの方がいい (kocchi no hou ga ii, 'this one is better')
• 歩く (aruku, 'to walk') → 歩いた方がいい (aruita hou ga ii, 'it's better to walk')
• 夏 (natsu, 'summer') → 夏の方が好き (natsu no hou ga suki, 'I like summer more')

Note: For nouns: A の方が. For verbs (advice): た-form + 方がいい = 'you should'. ずっと (zutto, 'much more') intensifies the comparison. This song's line powerfully says lies hurt MORE than the truth.
Verb stem + は + しない is a strong, often defiant negation: 'won't (do that), no way'. かないはしない 'no enemy can stand a chance'; 捨てはしない 'I won't throw it away'. Stronger than plain 〜ない.
explanation.es: Raíz del verbo + は + しない es negación enfática, a menudo desafiante. かないはしない 'ningún enemigo está a la altura'; 捨てはしない 'no lo voy a tirar'. Más fuerte que 〜ない.
explanation.pt-BR: Radical do verbo + は + しない é negação enfática, frequentemente desafiadora. かないはしない 'nenhum inimigo é páreo'; 捨てはしない 'não vou jogar fora'. Mais forte que 〜ない.

explanation.en:
How it works: Take the verb masu-stem and add はじめる (hajimeru, 'to begin'). This creates a compound verb meaning 'to begin doing something'.

Example from this song: つかみはじめた (tsukami hajimeta) = 'began to grasp' — from つかむ (tsukamu, 'to grasp') → つかみ (tsukami, masu-stem) + はじめた (hajimeta, past of hajimeru)

More examples:
• 降る (furu, 'to fall') → 降りはじめる (furi hajimeru, 'begin to fall — rain starting')
• 読む (yomu, 'to read') → 読みはじめる (yomi hajimeru, 'begin to read')
• 分かる (wakaru, 'to understand') → 分かりはじめる (wakari hajimeru, 'begin to understand')

Note: Compare with 〜だす (dasu), which also means 'begin to' but implies a more sudden or unexpected start. はじめる is a gradual, intentional beginning.

name: 〜はずのない (hazu no nai - not supposed to)

explanation.en:
Expresses that something was not supposed to happen, that it goes against expectations. はず (hazu) means "supposed to" and のない (no nai) negates it.

How it works:
Verb dictionary form + はず (hazu) + の (no) + ない (nai). It modifies a noun: "a [noun] that was not supposed to [verb]."

Example from this song:
来るはずのない朝 (kuru hazu no nai asa, "A morning that was never supposed to come")

More examples:
- 失敗するはずのないテスト (shippai suru hazu no nai tesuto, "A test that was not supposed to be failed")
- ここにあるはずのない鍵 (koko ni aru hazu no nai kagi, "A key that shouldn’t be here")
- 泣くはずのない彼が泣いた (naku hazu no nai kare ga naita, "He cried, though he wasn’t supposed to")

name: 〜はずのない (hazu no nai) — should not have / impossible that

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb た-form (ta-form) + はずのない (hazu no nai) means "should not have ~" or "it's impossible that ~." はず (hazu) expresses expectation, and のない (no nai) negates it — the expectation was that it could not happen, yet it did. This expresses surprise at something unexpected.

Example from this song:
交わしたはずのない (kawashita hazu no nai) — "shouldn't have exchanged"
The singer is surprised by a connection or promise that logically should not exist.

More examples:
• ここに置いたはずのない鍵 (koko ni oita hazu no nai kagi) — "a key that shouldn't have been placed here"
• 会ったはずのない人 (atta hazu no nai hito) — "a person I shouldn't have met"
• 知っているはずのない情報 (shitte iru hazu no nai jouhou) — "information they shouldn't know"

name: 〜ばいい (it's fine if you / just do X)

explanation.en: Conditional 〜ば + いい literally 'if X then it's good' = 'just do X / it'll be fine to do X'. Gentle permission or encouragement: 決めればいい ('it's fine to just decide'). Adding さ at the end softens it further into reassurance.
explanation.es: Condicional 〜ば + いい significa 'si X, entonces bien' = 'basta con hacer X / hazlo y ya'. Permiso/aliento suave: 決めればいい. Con さ al final suena aún más reconfortante.
explanation.pt-BR: Condicional 〜ば + いい significa 'se X, então tudo bem' = 'é só fazer X / pode fazer X'. Permissão ou incentivo suave: 決めればいい. Com さ no fim, vira tom mais reconfortante.

explanation.en:
How it works: Place ばかり (bakari) or its casual form ばっか (bakka) after a past tense verb to mean 'just did' or after a noun to mean 'only/nothing but'. It indicates exclusivity or recency.

Example from this song: 始まったばっか (hajimatta bakka) = 'just started' — from 始まった (hajimatta, 'started') + ばっか (bakka, 'just')

More examples:
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べたばかり (tabeta bakari, 'just ate')
• 文句 (monku, 'complaints') → 文句ばかり言う (monku bakari iu, 'do nothing but complain')
• 来た (kita, 'came') → 来たばっかり (kita bakkari, 'just arrived')

Note: た + ばかり = 'just did' (recency). ばかり with nouns = 'only/nothing but'. ばっか/ばっかり are casual contractions. 遊んでばかりいる (asonde bakari iru, 'do nothing but play').

How it works: べき (beki) attaches to the dictionary form of a verb to express 'should' or 'ought to.' It indicates a moral obligation or something that is expected.

Example from this song: 愛されるべき (aisareru beki) = 'should be loved' — from 愛される (aisareru, 'to be loved', passive of 愛する) + べき (beki)

More examples:
• 行くべきだ (iku beki da, 'should go') — from 行く (iku, 'to go')
• 知るべきことだ (shiru beki koto da, 'something you should know') — from 知る (shiru, 'to know')
• やるべきことをやる (yaru beki koto o yaru, 'do what should be done') — from やる (yaru, 'to do')

Note: べき is stronger than ほうがいい (hou ga ii, 'it would be better'). The exception is する → するべき or すべき (both are correct). べき implies duty or moral correctness.

name: 〜ますように (may it be that... — wish form)

explanation.en: Verb + ますように expresses a wish: 雨が湿らせますように = 'may the rain dampen it'; 合格しますように ('may I pass'); 元気でいますように ('may you stay well'). Standard wording on tanabata strips and prayer plaques (絵馬).
explanation.es: Verbo + ますように expresa un deseo: 雨が湿らせますように, 合格しますように, 元気でいますように. Forma estándar en tiras del tanabata y ema (tablillas votivas).
explanation.pt-BR: Verbo + ますように exprime um desejo: 雨が湿らせますように, 合格しますように, 元気でいますように. Frase padrão em tiras do tanabata e ema (placas de oração).

explanation.en: Noun + まみれ means 'covered in / drenched in'. Like だらけ but specifically for sticky/wet things — blood, mud, sweat, oil. Aqua Timez extends it to abstract nouns: 挫折まみれ 'covered in setbacks'.
explanation.es: Sustantivo + まみれ significa 'cubierto de / empapado en'. Similar a だらけ, pero para cosas pegajosas/húmedas. 挫折まみれ 'cubierto de fracasos'.
explanation.pt-BR: Substantivo + まみれ significa 'coberto de / banhado em'. Parecido com だらけ mas mais para líquidos/grude. 挫折まみれ 'coberto de fracassos'.

name: 〜まるで...のように (marude... no you ni: just like)

explanation.en:
How it works: まるで (marude) means 'just like' and pairs with のように (no you ni) or みたいに (mitai ni) to create vivid similes. It emphasizes how closely something resembles something else.

Example from this song: まるで人生だから (marude jinsei dakara) = 'because it's just like life' — comparing the situation to life itself, from 人生 (jinsei, 'life')

More examples:
• まるで映画のように (marude eiga no you ni, 'just like a movie') — from 映画 (eiga, 'movie')
• まるで夢のようだ (marude yume no you da, 'it's just like a dream') — from 夢 (yume, 'dream')
• まるで別人のように変わった (marude betsujin no you ni kawatta, 'changed as if a different person')

Note: まるで adds emphasis to the comparison. Without まるで, のように still works but sounds less dramatic. みたいに is the casual equivalent of のように.

name: 〜みたいだ (it seems like; it's like)

explanation.en:
How it works: Add みたいだ (mitai da) after a noun, verb, or adjective to express resemblance or conjecture — 'it seems like X' or 'it's like X'. This is the casual equivalent of ようだ.

Example from this song: The song uses みたいだ to compare feelings and situations to something familiar, creating vivid imagery.

More examples:
• 夢 (yume, 'dream') → 夢みたいだ (yume mitai da, 'it's like a dream')
• 死んだ (shinda, 'died') → 死んだみたいだ (shinda mitai da, 'it seems like it died')
• 春 (haru, 'spring') → 春みたいだ (haru mitai da, 'it's like spring')

Note: Before a noun, use みたいな: 夢みたいな世界 (yume mitai na sekai, 'a world like a dream'). Before a verb, use みたいに: 鳥みたいに飛ぶ (tori mitai ni tobu, 'fly like a bird').

How it works:
The pattern X + も (mo) + Y + も (mo) means "both X and Y" or "X as well as Y." It emphasizes that multiple things share the same quality or are included equally. It can also be used with negatives to mean "neither X nor Y" when followed by a negative verb.

Example from this song:
The singer lists multiple things that are equally important or equally lost, using も...も to give them equal weight.

More examples:
• 日本語も英語も話せる (nihongo mo eigo mo hanaseru) — "can speak both Japanese and English"
• 時間もお金もない (jikan mo okane mo nai) — "have neither time nor money"
• 父も母も元気です (chichi mo haha mo genki desu) — "both my father and mother are well"

A literary/poetic form of 〜ていく (te iku), expressing a gradual change moving away from the speaker. Common in poetry and song lyrics.

How it works:
Attach ゆく (yuku) to the masu-stem of a verb. It replaces the more casual ていく (te iku).

Example from this song:
奪われゆく生命 (ubarare yuku seimei, "Lives being gradually taken away")

More examples:
- 消えゆく光 (kie yuku hikari, "Light fading away")
- 過ぎゆく時 (sugi yuku toki, "Time passing by")
- 変わりゆく世界 (kawari yuku sekai, "A world that is changing")

name: 〜ようで (you de) — as if / it seems like

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb plain form + ようで (you de) means "as if ~" or "it seems like ~ and..." The で (de) is the て-form of だ (da), allowing this simile to connect to another clause. It describes the appearance or impression of something while continuing the sentence.

Example from this song:
しみ込むようで (shimi komu you de) — "as if soaking in"
The feeling is described as seeping deeply into the singer's heart.

More examples:
• 夢のようで信じられない (yume no you de shinjirarenai) — "it's like a dream and I can't believe it"
• 終わりのないようで疲れた (owari no nai you de tsukareta) — "it seemed endless and I got tired"
• 時間が止まったようで静かだった (jikan ga tomatta you de shizuka datta) — "it was as if time stopped and it was quiet"

name: 〜ようとして (you to shite) — trying to

explanation.en:
How it works:
The pattern Verb volitional form + とする (to suru) means "to try to ~" or "to be about to ~." The て-form version, ようとして (you to shite), connects this attempt to what happens next. It captures the moment of effort or intention, often when the attempt is difficult or interrupted.

Example from this song:
見つけ出そうとして (mitsuke dasou to shite) — "trying to find"
The singer is making an effort to discover something.

More examples:
• 逃げようとしたが、捕まった (nigeyou to shita ga, tsukamatta) — "tried to escape but was caught"
• ドアを開けようとしている (doa o akeyou to shite iru) — "is trying to open the door"
• 立ち上がろうとして転んだ (tachiagaro to shite koronda) — "tried to stand up and fell"
